AB_raw: The 21 cm hydrogen line offers a practical way to introduce students to radio astronomy, spectral analysis, and Doppler shifts using authentic data from the Milky Way. However, the technical and financial barriers of conventional hydrogen-line detection systems often limit accessibility, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study presents the design, implementation, and field testing of a low-cost, autonomous radio telescope system based on a Raspberry Pi and software-defined radio for detecting Doppler-shifted hydrogen emission near 1420.405 MHz. Field trials conducted in Jasaan, Misamis Oriental, Philippines demonstrate detection of a hydrogen-line peak with both redshifted and blueshifted cases over different observing times. The results support the feasibility of an affordable and replicable set-up for physics education, public outreach, and introductory research activities. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: We present a simple algebraic derivation of the equation for a line of best fit. TI: IT ALL BEGAN WITH H—A CENTURY OF QUANTUM MECHANICS: FROM PLANCK TO TODAY’S QUANTUM TECHNOLOGIES
AB_raw: Quantum mechanics has revolutionised our understanding of reality. At the heart of this theory lies Planck’s constant h, which plays a fundamental role in describing the behaviour of matter on the smallest scales. In this paper we present a teaching approach that combines a concise historical overview of the origin of h with a simple experiment in which students determine its value from measurements on a photovoltaic panel. The article integrates methodologies from Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics and problem-based learning to demonstrate how contemporary educational techniques can not only aid in understanding quantum concepts, but also enable the experimental determination of one of the most fundamental constants of nature. Using low-cost components available in school and introductory university laboratories, students measure the threshold voltage of a photovoltaic cell for different wavelengths of light and, by analysing the linear dependence of the electron energy e U on c / λ to obtain an experimental estimate of h. In contrast to other works where light-emitting diodes have been used to determine Planck’s constant (Chakarvarti and Sharma 1988 Phys. Educ. 23 416; Ward 2013 Phys. Educ. 48 20–1; Morton and Abraham 1986 Phys. Educ. 21 414; Korpal et al 2023 Phys. Educ. 58 045003), this article presents a method of experimentally determining h, by measuring the threshold voltage of a photovoltaic panel as a function of the frequency of incident light. The proposed experiment can be easily conducted in a school setting, for example as a group project under the guidance of a teacher. It illustrates that core quantum concepts can be explored experimentally even at the introductory level. Furthermore, this experiment can complement university-level lectures or laboratory courses. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd.

AB_raw: This study aimed to develop and validate a constructed-response assessment to measure analytical thinking skills in the context of particle dynamics. Grounded in Sternberg’s theory of analytical intelligence, the instrument comprised seven open-ended items aligned with indicators such as analysing, critiquing, evaluating, explaining, logical reasoning, drawing conclusions, and sorting. A five-point rubric was developed for each item to evaluate the accuracy, depth, and logical coherence of student responses. Content validity was established through expert judgment involving six specialists in learning evaluation and physics, using Aiken’s V index. The instrument was pilot-tested with 106 undergraduate students from the Physics Education Program, and data were analysed using the Rasch model. All items demonstrated good fit (infit/outfit mean square 0.5–1.5) and high item reliability (0.99), while person reliability was moderately acceptable (0.79). The wright map confirmed good targeting, though a ceiling effect suggested limited challenge for high-performing students. Unidimensionality assumptions were satisfied, supporting construct validity. The findings provide empirical support for a theoretically grounded instrument that captures analytical thinking in physics and suggest directions for extending the assessment to broader science domains and instructional contexts. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: HOW INTERNAL FORCES INDIRECTLY AFFECT THE ACCELERATION OF A SYSTEM: EXAMPLE AND INSIGHTS
AB_raw: The influence of internal forces in classical mechanics is often overlooked in textbooks, despite their crucial role in shaping a system’s response to external forces. In this study, we examine a simple two-body system—a mass on a table connected by a string to a hanging mass—to highlight how internal tension affects acceleration. By varying the angle of the string, we explore how the transmission of force changes in both frictionless and frictional scenarios. Our analysis reveals that in the absence of friction, internal tension merely distributes the driving force, whereas in the presence of friction, it actively alters the normal force, thereby modifying resistive forces. These findings provide new insights into multi-body dynamics and suggest that a deeper emphasis on internal forces in introductory physics courses could enhance the presentation of Newtonian mechanics. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AF: HORTA-RANGEL FRANCISCO ANTONIO;VERA FRANCISCO;ORTIZ MANUEL;RIVERA RODRIGO
AB_raw: Here we explain a straightforward method to measure the polarity of charged objects for introductory experiments of electricity. The device consists of two LEDs connected in parallel but opposite directions. The legs at one side are joined by twisting them and act as an antenna, and the two legs at the other side are twisted to one side of a 470 kΩ resistor. AB_raw: This paper presents a theoretical and epistemological reflection on the identity of physics education and on the professional practice of the physics teacher, with particular emphasis on secondary schooling. The paper discusses implications for inquiry-, problem- and project-oriented approaches and argues for lean and conceptually coherent curricula organised around meaningful questions rather than exhaustive topic lists. By prioritising epistemological integrity over content accumulation, this work highlights physics education as a formative space for the development of scientific thinking. AB_raw: L-squares, or carpenter’s squares, offer a simple and inexpensive system for introducing students to static equilibrium and mechanical stability. We present a hierarchy of theoretical models, ranging from idealised to realistic, that predict the equilibrium angle of the longer arm with respect to the vertical as a function of geometry, including arm thickness and length ratio, assuming identical thickness and mass density for both arms and ideal contact with the support. The analysis uses the principle of virtual work, which provides an alternative to traditional force-based methods. By eliminating the need to explicitly calculate unknown reaction forces, this principle highlights the essential role of geometry and applied forces in equilibrium, thereby promoting conceptual understanding and offering students a clearer insight into the underlying mechanics. These models are validated through accessible experiments using low-cost, 3D-printed or laser-cut L-squares. A simple, classroom-ready experimental setup is described, allowing students to test theoretical predictions by observing how geometry influences stability. This approach provides a hands-on opportunity to confront theory with practice, explore stability thresholds and understand the relationship between idealised models and real systems. The experimental framework can also be adapted to design classroom activities. © 2025 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd.

AB_raw: Joule’s paddle wheel experiment has become famous in the history of physics. Illustrations of the experiment have appeared in textbooks since the 19th century. However, the textbook diagrams of Joule’s experiment differ from each other, and most differ from the original diagram. The differences appear to be significant. The question of whether the results of the experiments are the same in each of the experimental configurations is addressed in this paper. In order to answer this question, a replica of the original calorimeter was built. This comparison gives us a new insight into the potential energy transformed into heat. © 2025 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd.

AB_raw: Transmission lines play a crucial role in radio-frequency energy transmission between source and load. These systems connect essential physical phenomena like the formation of standing waves and the attenuation of electromagnetic waves in material media with practical considerations such as impedance matching and signal integrity. The absence of impedance matching between the line and load leads to a modulated amplitude in the resulting signal owing to interference between the injected and reflected signals. Here, we present an experiment utilizing an Arduino platform as a signal generator and a data acquisition interface to analyze a radio frequency transmission line. By employing a few-meter-long coaxial cable as the transmission line and a digital oscilloscope with a high sampling rate (several giga-samples per second), we demonstrate how to determine the reflection coefficient as a function of the load impedance. TI: DEMONSTRATION EXPERIMENT FOR OBSERVING HAIDINGER’S INTERFERENCE RINGS USING MICROPARTICLES DEPOSITED ON REFLECTIVE SURFACES
AB_raw: A demonstration experiment for observing Haidinger’s interference rings (fringes of equal inclination) is proposed and experimentally implemented. The method uses microparticles deposited on the reflective surfaces of plane-parallel glass plates or flat mirrors. These particles act as localised secondary sources, converting the angular interference structure into a directly observable ring pattern on a screen in the far field. While similar observations have been reported for dusty mirrors, this work extends the technique to glass plates. We demonstrate that microparticles on both surfaces introduce additional coherent scattering paths exhibiting a similar angular phase dependence, leading to a pronounced enhancement of fringe visibility without altering the geometric arrangement of the rings. The experiment employs inexpensive and readily available equipment, such as a low-power semiconductor laser pointer, a glass plate, and a mirror, enabling stable interference patterns with high fringe visibility to be observed under standard classroom lighting. Quantitative analysis of the interference patterns is presented, including measurements of ring radii and determination of the glass plate thickness. The shifts of selected ring radii provide a direct and intuitive demonstration of the wavelength dependence of interference, allowing students to explore optical dispersion without the need for spectrometers. By combining classical interferometry with accessible experimental techniques and digital data processing, this approach makes Haidinger’s fringes readily observable and pedagogically effective for both secondary school and university laboratory exercises. © 2026 The Author(s). This paper offers recommendations for optimizing AI-assisted learning, fostering critical thinking, and adapting assessment practices to balance AI’s educational benefits with academic integrity. AB_raw: Brian Greene’s presidents-on-a-train thought experiment vividly illustrates the relativity of simultaneity in special relativity: two presidents seated at opposite ends of a moving train sign a peace treaty simultaneously in the train frame, while ground observers conclude that the signings were not simultaneous. This paper introduces a mirror arrangement at the train’s centre that reflects light from both signings outward toward the ground observers. The mirror creates an apparent paradox: the same observers who infer non-simultaneity from Greene’s original analysis now receive mirror-reflected signals together, apparently indicating simultaneity. The resolution is that the mirror cancels two asymmetries. Light from the earlier of the two presidential signings takes longer to reach the train-centre mirror, while light from the later signing takes less time. The example provides a compact classroom illustration of the distinction between what observers see and what they observe, where observing means reasoning from visual signals to physical conclusions. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: CORRECTING THE ROLLING SHUTTER EFFECT IN A VIDEO ANALYSIS EXPERIMENT
AB_raw: The rolling shutter effect, a well-known source of distortion in pictures captured with sensors that acquire the image line by line rather than at a single instant, significantly impacts video analysis, a common technique in introductory physics labs for studying motion. When a decelerating rotational motion is recorded with such sensors, the measured angular velocity exhibits pronounced oscillations, rather than a uniform decrease. However, these artifacts can be eliminated by advancing or retarding the timestamp of each video frame. This correction, which involves calculating the derivative of data with non-uniformly spaced timestamps (a task achievable through straightforward methods), provides students with a valuable opportunity to understand the necessity of identifying and correcting sensor-induced artifacts. While the rolling shutter effect also introduces errors in projectile motion experiments, including a 4% overestimation of the free-fall acceleration g, its impact is less pronounced than in rotational motion scenarios. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS OF THE USE OF VR IN PHYSICS LEARNING: BEHAVIOURAL INTENTION ANALYSIS BASED ON DIFFERENCES IN GENDER, AGE, AND EXPERIENCE
AB_raw: Physics is often perceived as a difficult subject due to its abstract nature, which calls for innovative media such as virtual reality (VR) to enhance students’ conceptual understanding. This study aims to analyse students’ perceptions of VR in physics learning and to identify factors influencing behavioural intention (BI) based on differences in gender, age, and prior VR experience. A quantitative survey with a cross-sectional design involved 213 physics education students at a state university in Tasikmalaya, Indonesia. The research instrument was a questionnaire measuring performance expectancy (PE), effort expectancy (EE), social influence (SI), and BI, analysed using structural equation modelling with SmartPLS version 4.0.9.9. The results show that, overall, students have a positive perception of VR use (average 73%, categorized as high). All three constructs—PE, EE, and SI—significantly influenced BI, with PE emerging as the strongest predictor. Multi-group analysis revealed that gender and age did not moderate the relationships among the variables, while prior experience with VR in physics learning significantly strengthened the predictive relationships with BI. The findings highlight the importance of improving infrastructure, providing teacher training, and fostering social support to enhance VR adoption in physics learning, while also offering valuable insights for policymakers and educational technology developers. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This work presents a pedagogical approach for introducing synchronization phenomena in high school physics education through the Kuramoto model, contributing to complex systems education at the secondary level. Synchronization occurs when coupled oscillators, initially out of phase, begin to oscillate in phase with a common frequency due to coupling between their constituent elements. This phenomenon is widely observed in nature and artificial systems, from firefly flashing patterns to mechanical metronomes, yet remains largely absent from secondary education curricula. We propose a two-stage methodology to make this complex concept accessible to high school students. The first stage involves experimental investigation using video analysis with Tracker software to study coupled metronomes, allowing students to observe phase relationships and measure synchronization dynamics. The second stage utilizes computational simulations to explore the mathematical framework of the Kuramoto model and examine various coupling scenarios. This approach bridges the gap between advanced physics concepts typically reserved for university-level courses and secondary education, enabling educators to effectively teach sophisticated phenomena from complex systems at the high school level. The methodology integrates theoretical understanding with hands-on experimentation and computational modelling, providing students with multiple perspectives on synchronization phenomena. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: QUANTUM PHYSICS MEETS COMPUTATIONAL THINKING: ACCESSING QUANTUM MECHANICS WITH PYTHON-BASED COMPUTATIONAL EXERCISES
AB_raw: Learning quantum mechanics (QMs) poses unique challenges due to its abstract, unintuitive nature and departure from classical physics paradigms. In this context, computational methods hold potential not only for improving conceptual understanding but also for addressing the motivational difficulties often encountered in learning QMs. This study investigates how computational Python exercises impact students’ experiences and conceptual understanding in a massive open online course designed for high school and early undergraduate students. Data was collected using an online questionnaire that probed the understanding of QMs concepts and computational methods. The 48 participants were randomly assigned to two groups that completed the questionnaire and the computational exercises in a different order. Students’ answers were studied using content analysis, rubrics, and statistical methods. The results suggest that while computational methods offer valuable means for concretizing abstract QM ideas, attention must be paid to how computational models are presented, particularly for students with limited computational background. This study provides preliminary evidence that a short, carefully designed computational intervention can positively influence students’ views on computational thinking. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: Ohm’s law is traditionally verified in physics laboratories under steady-state conditions by varying resistance and measuring corresponding current–voltage pairs. While operationally effective, this approach often obscures the instantaneous and local nature of Ohm’s law and encourages the misconception that the law is valid only for constant currents. In this article, a time-domain verification of Ohm’s law is presented using a fixed resistor in a series resistor (R)-capacitor (C) circuit. The charging and discharging of a capacitor driven by a low-voltage DC source are studied by simultaneously measuring voltage and current as functions of time. Experimental voltage–time and current–time data exhibit the expected exponential behaviour, while the voltage–current plots (voltage versus corresponding current at any instant) obtained from measurements taken at different times during charging and discharging yield straight lines with nearly identical slopes. The results demonstrate that, despite the circuit being globally non-Ohmic, the variation of voltage and current through the resistor obeys Ohm’s law instantaneously at all times. The experiment provides a complementary, conceptually rich alternative to the conventional rheostat-based verification of Ohm’s law, while the present method offers a conceptually richer yet experimentally easier means of understanding the instantaneous and local nature of Ohm’s law in time-dependent circuits. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. These findings suggest that the learning environment effectively supports sustained conceptual understanding of the greenhouse effect in the target age group. AB_raw: There are various locations in the vicinity of the Earth’s orbit around the Sun where centripetal and centrifugal forces are balanced and spacecraft are able to orbit the Sun at the same period as the Earth. SOHO provides high resolution images of the Sun, and DSCOVR provides an early warning of coronal mass ejections, and detailed images of the Earth. In a halo orbit, the orthogonal components of the spacecraft-Sun and spacecraft-Earth force vectors provide the centripetal force enabling a spacecraft to orbit a point in space. This paper illustrates how a visual programming environment called Scratch can serve as an accessible and low-barrier platform for integrating computational modeling into K-16 physics instruction. A comprehensive CT framework developed specifically for physics education was employed as an analytic lens to articulate the CT practices targeted by the activity across the model design, construction, testing, and inquiry stages. The activity promotes meta-modeling knowledge among students by making explicit the simplifying assumptions of models and inviting iterative testing and refinement. The design features that enhance usability of the model (e.g. manipulating variables through sliders, real-time plotting of the motion) were discussed along with some suggestions to extend the model to inquire about different research questions. TI: PLANCK’S CONSTANT DETERMINATION FROM FERRY’S BLACK-BODY RADIATION: A STRAIGHTFORWARD METHOD
AB_raw: This article presents a simple and straightforward approach for determining Planck’s constant by examining the radiation emitted from a Ferry-like black body configured as a hemisphere. The Ferry black body was maintained at a constant temperature of ∼98.5 °C through the continuous flow of steam within a double-walled structure. The radiation emitted from the inner blackened surface and through a small aperture at the bottom was captured by a sensitive T-type double-junction thermocouple. One junction of the thermocouple was connected to a silver disc to capture the maximum radiations emitted from the aperture, while the other junction was maintained at room temperature in silicon oil. The variation in thermo-electromotive force (E.M.F.) across the double junction was recorded as a thermal sensing signal when the junction attached to the silver disc was exposed to the black body radiation. For calibration of the double junction, the second junction was heated in silicon oil while the silver disc junction was maintained at room temperature, and the thermo-E.M.F. was recorded as a function of temperature, which was measured using a mercury thermometer. The Planck’s constant obtained through this method was approximately 6.9 × 10 − 34 Js, which closely aligns with the standard value of ∼ 6.626 × 10 − 34 Js. The close correspondence between the measured and standard values of Planck’s constant confirms the effectiveness of this method. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: ROLLING MARBLES, ENERGY CONSERVATION, AND THE FRONTIERS OF SCIENCE
AB_raw: A simple classroom experiment is described that uses a marble rolling down an inclined plane to teach students the relationship between gravitational potential energy, and linear and rotational kinetic energy. A marble is rolled down a 1 m-long aluminium channel set at five inclinations, and a mobile phone video camera used to measure the time for the marble to roll from the top to the bottom of the track. Uniform acceleration of the marble is assumed. The acceleration time is used to calculate the final linear velocity and kinetic energy knowing the mass of the marble. The linear velocity is used to calculate the angular velocity of the marble, assuming no slippage. The sum of the linear and rotation energies is plotted against initial potential energy. The experiment is useful for teaching students about conservation of energy, and the role this has played in major discoveries in physics, for example the discovery of the neutrino, dark matter, and dark energy. © 2026 The Author(s). AB_raw: In this paper we introduce a novel method to teach momentum by using direct measurements. The basic idea is to define an ordering relation ‘more momentum than’ in hands-on collision tests. When we let two pendulum masses collide inelastically head-on we can directly observe whether two objects rest jointly or if one overruns the other. We can set up a test object with a number of mass units and, with known starting heights for a pendulum, we can also set up multiples of a unit velocity. In the collision test we can systematically increase the number of mass units of a reference pendulum with fixed unit velocity until the case, that the two masses rest jointly. By counting these momentum units we can quantify the momentum with respect to velocity and mass. Finally by analysing this measurement principle in vivid thought experiments on the impossible construction of perpetual motion machines we deduce the momentum conservation. We give examples that were tested and evaluated in high school physics classes. © 2025 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd.

TI: JUMPING INTO THE SECOND NEWTON LAW: CONCEPTUALIZATION OF THE LANDING PROCESS
AB_raw: The second Newton law is one of the basic laws in classical mechanics and therefore, demands deep conceptual understanding by physics learners. This, however, frequently is not the situation. Precisely, students experience difficulties applying Newton Laws in the analysis of real life situations. An interesting real-world context ruled by the principles of classical mechanics is the world of acrobatics and parkour. Here almost every jump creates the ‘Wow’ affect and hence is probable to draw the attention of learners; thus, inspiring a true curiosity regarding its underlying physics principles. Each acrobatic jump requires the skill of safe landing which is the process of zeroing a jumpers’ velocity within a certain time period. The second Newton law describes this situation. In the present study, we analyse a real jump and employ it as a real life case for 5 clinical interviews and 3 focus-group interviews (conducted as whole class dialogic discussions)—69 participants in total. The interviews’ analysis yielded three kinds of misconceptions. We further discuss these misconceptions and suggest practical ways for their review. We believe that physics teaching and classical mechanics precisely, should be based on such practical examples, which are likely to arouse curiosity on the one hand, and can be easily experienced by most of the learners. In our case, the tool is always accessible; it is the body of every one of us. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This study aims to integrate and evaluate the effectiveness of a metaverse Spatial.io-based pre-laboratory environment in enhancing students’ conceptual understanding of Newton’s laws. Conventional pre-laboratory media are often passive and provide limited opportunities for immersive, interactive preparation, which may restrict students’ ability to develop a robust conceptual foundation before examination. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was employed, involving two groups of physics education students (experimental n = 30; control n = 30). Conceptual understanding was assessed using a validated and reliable test instrument. The results indicate that the experimental group engaging with Spatial.io achieved significantly greater improvement in conceptual understanding than the control group using 2D video media, with an independent sample t-test showing a significant difference in normalizedgains (t (58) = −3.199, p = 0.002). These findings suggest that immersive pre-laboratory experience can better facilitate active cognitive engagement and support the formation of more concrete mental models of fundamental mechanics concepts. Overall, Spatial.io appears feasible and promising as an innovative pre-laboratory medium that bridges theory and practice in physics learning and offers a scalable approach to strengthening conceptual readiness before laboratory activities. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This study explored (mis)conceptions of ionizing radiation by using cloud chambers among four lay public groups: lower secondary school students, upper secondary school students, primary teacher students, and shopping mall customers. Ionizing radiation was most commonly associated with natural sources such as the Sun, as well as risks like cancer and nuclear accidents. However, widespread misconceptions were evident, including the belief that mobile phones are significant sources of ionizing radiation. Upper secondary school students perceived ionizing radiation as more harmful compared to the lower secondary school students. Shopping mall customers associated ionizing radiation with threats but did not consider it particularly harmful. With a cloud chamber demonstration primary teacher students and shopping mall customers gained insights into the prevalence of ionizing radiation and the relative harmlessness of background radiation, while upper secondary students did not report this takeaway. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This study investigates the influence of e-readiness skills (ERS), physics literacy (PL), and self-efficacy (SE) on pre-service teachers’ misconceptions in physics. This study utilised a quantitative design using a survey method. Data were collected from 122 participants using validated instruments measuring ERS, SE, PL, and misconceptions. Descriptive results indicate high ERS and SE levels, moderate PL proficiency, and persistent misconceptions across several physics topics. Multiple linear regression analysis reveals that PL significantly predicts misconceptions, whereas ERS and SE show no significant effects. The model accounts for 16.5% of the variance in misconceptions, suggesting that content mastery exerts greater influence than digital readiness or teaching confidence. AB_raw: Teamwork is an essential skill for STEM students, but ensuring equitable workload distribution remains a challenge. We propose a token-based method to incentivise equal work sharing. Each team of size N receives 2 N+1 tokens, which students openly discuss how to divide amongst their teammates. Two tokens result in a full grade, while three tokens earn a bonus. This system is implemented in small, frequent team assignments, promoting immediate peer feedback for underperforming teammates. The ability to bank bonus tokens ahead of time also allows flexibility for students who have illnesses or emergencies. The token system was piloted with university undergraduates in an introductory engineering and an upper-level physics course, with surveys conducted at the 16-week semester’s start and end. Results showed that students’ perceptions of group work improved, teams using the token system had more equitable contributions compared to a control group, and students had mostly positive comments about the token system. A few students pointed out some deficiencies, especially social pressure to not penalise underperforming students. Based on survey data and the authors’ experience, we offer the following recommendations for instructors: provide in-class time for token discussions even if the assignments are submitted outside of class, be prepared to mediate conflicts, monitor groups for the social pressure to avoid penalties, set a semester cap of 100% for token points to avoid work hoarding, and be careful when using the system with continually reshuffled teams. AB_raw: This paper presents a portable and simple refractive index kit that lets students study refraction, refractive index, and the critical angle in both solids and liquids. In schools, refraction is typically taught using a ray box that produce bright and dim rays, making refraction hard to observe. In addition, the activity also requires drawing lines on paper to trace the rays, which is time consuming and slows the process of teaching and learning. To overcome this problem, the portable refractive index kit uses a monochromatic 532 nm laser beam with a rotating mount and a fixed protractor as the sample stage, making the rays easy to observe without paper tracing and speeding up the lesson. In addition, the kit also offers added value by including a liquid container that enables refractive-index studies of liquids using the same geometry as solids without changing the setup. These additions save time, improve repeatability, and enable clear measurements for both solids and liquids within a single lesson. Refractive index is estimated using Snell’s law from a straight-line Snell plot, and the critical angle for total internal reflection is used as a built-in check. The uncertainties of n, obtained from standard error analysis, range between ± 0.01 and ± 0.02 depending on the measurement method. This project contributed to physics education by providing a low cost, accurate and easy to obtain experimental kit for schools. AB_raw: A core concept of electrostatics at the university level is calculating the electric field of simple geometric objects with uniformly distributed charges. The conventional calculation technique involves dividing the object into many infinitesimal elements. The total electric field at a point is obtained by summing the electric fields generated by each element vectorially. Therefore, students are required to have prior knowledge of calculus, especially integration. However, based on my experience, some students do not understand why integration is necessary for this problem, often due to an insufficient calculus background. This research proposes an alternative teaching method for finding the electric field of simple geometric objects with uniformly distributed charges (such as a charged rod, ring, and disk). This method involves directly summing the electric fields from each element without using integration, encouraging students to understand the problem from a physics point of view. The calculations require a computer program to perform the summation of many elements, allowing teachers to introduce computer programming or available tools to help students with the calculations. AB_raw: The concept of spacetime often conflates mathematical form with physical meaning, obscuring the central role of proper time. This article argues that such ambiguity contributes to persistent difficulties in teaching relativity. Without grounding in proper time, students frequently misinterpret time itself and struggle with the relativity of simultaneity. To address this, the article reframes spacetime by placing proper time at the center—as the primary expression of physical change. Guided by the principle of light, the article reformulates the Minkowski metric equation in temporal units, which exposes its meaning as reflecting the intuitive observation that one experiences distant objects not as they are now, but as they were when their light departed. The article also interprets the metric equation by a metric triangle, a geometric construct that interprets coordinate time as the orthogonal sum of proper time (internal rhythm) and time latency (from spatial separation). This framework clarifies key conceptual distinctions—between proper and coordinate time, simultaneity, and the metric itself—offering a more coherent and physically grounded understanding of spacetime. © 2025 The Author(s). AB_raw: Productive failure engages students in a problem-solving phase that requires them to solve novel problems targeting yet-to-be-learned accepted ideas before the instruction phase. A few studies have explored students working individually during the instruction phase, where they diagnose a fictitious student’s erroneous examples; i.e. identify and explain classical errors embedded in them, by comparing these erroneous examples with worked examples involving a step-by-step description of the correct solutions (dubbed ‘ungraded-troubleshooting’ activity). In the current study, which was part of a larger project, seven 8th-grade classes from three different middle schools completed a pretest/intervention/posttest before studying simple electric circuits. The intervention consisted of two productive failure sessions targeting yet-to-be-learned accepted ideas. In the instruction phase of each session, the students in each class were randomly assigned to four activities, two of which were examined here: an ungraded-troubleshooting activity (49 students) and a graded-troubleshooting activity (50 students). It was hypothesized that students would show greater performance gains on the graded-troubleshooting activity that scaffolded the instruction phase by asking students to score erroneous examples on a rubric portraying the worked examples, in addition to diagnosing them. Contrary to predictions, the ungraded-troubleshooting activities led to better learning outcomes. The instructional implications and directions for future research are discussed. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. The proposed sequence introduces students to micro- and nanoscale structure through a crime scene investigation (CSI)-based scenario while engaging them in inquiry activities involving SEM image observation, comparison, and interpretation. The teaching sequence was designed according to the 5E instructional model and uses images of human hair samples provided by a Virtual-SEM simulation. Within the sequence, students are expected to investigate the structure of hair samples, identify morphological differences, collect measurements, and compare microstructural characteristics across SEM images. The instructional design integrates three key dimensions: familiarisation with inquiry-oriented investigation processes, introduction to SEM imaging and microstructural analysis, and active engagement in the learning process through a CSI-based scenario. Core activities include image observation, quantitative measurement, sample comparison, and evidence-based interpretation. A preliminary validation phase, conducted through a questionnaire administered to 30 science teachers, provided formative feedback on the pedagogical design and perceived learning benefits of the sequence. Teachers’ responses also highlighted practical considerations for classroom implementation, informing directions for further refinement. The next stage of the research will involve classroom implementation to examine the sequence’s educational impact on student learning outcomes. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This paper presents a laboratory experiment designed to help undergraduate engineering students distinguish between the general principle of energy conservation and the conditional conservation of mechanical energy. Using the accessible system of a vertically bouncing ball, the experiment employs temporal measurements of successive rebound intervals. From these measurements, students determine the coefficient of restitution and quantify mechanical-energy loss during impacts without relying on fitting procedures or image analysis. The experiment is configured to minimize the influence of air resistance through the choice of small, relatively dense balls and modest release heights, ensuring that energy dissipation is dominated by non-conservative processes during the collision. The activity was implemented on a large scale with approximately 400 first-year students across two study programs. Student results exhibit a high degree of reproducibility, with clear distinctions between rigid and soft impact surfaces. The experiment proved robust, conceptually transparent, and well aligned with the learning objective of clarifying the limitations of mechanical-energy conservation. TI: A LITERATURE REVIEW ON THE DEFINITION OF THE PHENOMENON OF REFRACTION OF LIGHT
AB_raw: Refraction of light is one of the important topics in physics education. Depending on how the refraction is defined, textbooks offer different opinions on whether light waves travel perpendicular to the interface between two media and undergo refraction when passing from one medium to another. We examined twenty-eight fundamental physics textbooks to reveal the differences of opinion in the literature regarding the definition of refraction of light in a single source. It was observed that the majority of textbooks (57.1%) defined refraction of light waves as “the change in direction at the interface.” Additionally, the refraction was randomly defined as “the change in average speed”, “the bending”, or “the transmission” of light when passing from one medium to another. Therefore, some textbooks thought that light waves were not refracted when their direction of travel was perpendicular to the surface, despite changes in the medium. AB_raw: In this paper a series of hands-on demonstrations is described to teach students about hydrostatic pressure and buoyancy using fish. Fish are neutrally buoyant and therefore do not need to expend energy to swim up or down, apart from overcoming friction between their scales and fins, and water. In a first demonstration, the increase in hydrostatic pressure with depth is felt when a hollow plastic cylinder less dense than water is pushed into a tall container of water. In a second demonstration, robot fish of different density are placed at the top of a 1 m tall transparent plastic tube and observed to swim down. A neutrally buoyant robot fish swims steadily to the bottom and is suspended in the water column when not swimming. A negatively buoyant fish sinks continuously to the bottom, and a positively buoyant fish fails to reach the bottom. Archimedes principle can be used to accurately measure and adjust the density of a robot fish as necessary. In a third experiment, a sinker is lowered into an aquarium demonstrating that the weight of an object is independent of depth. Buoyancy brings together physics and marine biology and therefore is a good STEM topic. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd.

AB_raw: This paper presents an integrated sequence of introductory physics laboratory activities designed to promote modelling, graphical analysis, and uncertainty reasoning. The approach combines pairs of complementary experiments for the determination of liquid density, the elastic constant of a spring, and gravitational acceleration, while emphasizing the common methodological framework used to analyze experimental data. In each case, theoretical relationships are reformulated into linear forms that allow experimental results to be interpreted through graphical models, with physical parameters obtained from the slopes of fitted lines. The activities also highlight the process of transforming nonlinear relationships into linear representations and comparing results obtained through independent methods. Rather than focusing solely on the numerical determination of physical constants, the proposed sequence emphasizes modelling, data interpretation, and the role of experimental uncertainty in evaluating physical models. Because the experiments rely on standard laboratory equipment and widely accessible measurement techniques, the framework can be readily implemented in undergraduate teaching laboratories to support the development of fundamental experimental skills. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: Understanding electrical circuits remains a persistent challenge in physics education, particularly in technical–vocational contexts where laboratory resources may be limited. This study investigates the impact of an inquiry-based instructional intervention using a black-box experimental methodology on students’ conceptual understanding, confidence, and motivation related to electrical circuit laws. The study was conducted in a technical secondary school in Angola, providing evidence from an educational context that remains underrepresented in physics education research. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control group design was implemented with 70 Grade 11 students (typically aged 16–17 years) enrolled in an Energy and Electrical Installations programme. The experimental group engaged in hands-on black-box investigations designed to promote model-based reasoning using Ohm’s Law and Kirchhoff’s Laws, while the control group received traditional lecture-based instruction. Students’ responses were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analysed using Mann–Whitney U and Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests. Pre-test results showed no statistically significant differences between groups (p > 0.05), indicating comparable initial levels. After the intervention, statistically significant differences were observed between groups across all measured constructs (Q1–Q3: p < 0.001; Q4: p = 0.012). Effect-size analysis revealed large effects for confidence, application of circuit laws, and conceptual understanding (r = 0.72–0.75) and a moderate effect for motivation (r = 0.30). Additional post-test survey items applied only to the experimental group indicated very positive student perceptions of the activity (Q5 mean = 4.89, SD = 0.32; Q6 mean = 4.97, SD = 0.17). These results suggest that black-box experimental activities provide an effective and low-cost strategy for promoting inquiry-based learning and improving conceptual understanding of electrical circuits in resource-constrained technical education environments. The findings highlight the potential of black-box investigations as an accessible experimental strategy for teaching electrical circuits in technical and secondary physics classrooms. © 2026 The Author(s). AB_raw: The role of thought experiments in the teaching of experimental sciences and the academic progress of students has been discussed. The purpose of this research was to investigate the effect of teaching mechanical (dynamic) concepts with a thought experiment approach on academic progress, cognitive learning levels, and cognitive skills (cognitive flexibility and self-regulation skills) of students. This research was quantitative and quasi-experimental conducted with a pre-test-post-test design with experimental and control groups. The statistical population of this research was all 12th-grade female students in the city of Karaj, Alborz province of Iran in the academic year 2023-2024. The research sample included 55 randomly selected students. The measurement tools were a researcher-made test to assess academic progress, the cognitive flexibility questionnaire of Dennis and Vander Wall (2010 Cogn. Ther. Res. 34 241-53) to measure cognitive flexibility, and the learning strategies questionnaire (Pintrich and De Groot 1990) to measure self-regulation skills of students. Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the instruments is 0.70, 0.75, and 0.76 respectively. In this research, 6 thought experiments were discussed in six different 75 min training sessions. The data collected in this research were analyzed by ANCOVA and independent t-test. The results of the research showed the positive effect of the thought experiment on students’ academic progress and cognitive skills (cognitive flexibility and self-regulation skills). It was found that the experimental group had higher development in academic achievement and cognitive levels than the control group. It was also observed that despite the academic progress of the control group compared to their pre-test, they had a downward trend in cognitive flexibility and self-regulation skills. The experimental group, however, made progress in cognitive levels, academic achievement, cognitive flexibility and self-regulation. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: DETERMINATION OF THE MUTUAL INDUCTIVENESS COEFFICIENT OF COILS ON A FERROMAGNETIC CORE
AB_raw: In ferromagnetic cores, the magnetic field inside a toroid is spatially non-uniform, and the relative magnetic permeability μ(H) depends nonlinearly on the magnetic field strength H. In electromagnetism courses, when determining mutual inductance, it is usually assumed that the relative magnetic permeability of the core material is constant, which significantly affects the calculated values of mutual inductance. In the proposed method for determining mutual inductance, a graphical analysis of the function μ(H)/H is used to account for the non-uniform distribution of the magnetic field and magnetization in a toroidal core. When determining the magnetic flux through the cross-section of the core, integration with respect to the magnetic field strength is employed. Since an analytical expression for the relative magnetic permeability μ(H) is not available and is given graphically, the required integrals are evaluated graphically. The method is illustrated by calculation examples for a toroidal core made of American Rolling Mill Company iron. The results show that the mutual inductance depends on the current in the primary coil, the number of turns, and the ratio of the outer to inner radii of the core. A comparison with the method based on a constant relative magnetic permeability demonstrates that such an approach can lead to significant errors, especially in regimes where the magnetic field varies considerably across the core cross-section. The proposed method accounts for the nonlinearity of the magnetic properties of the ferromagnetic core and the non-uniformity of the magnetic field. It helps students relate theoretical concepts to the experimental properties of materials. The use of digital tools for determining the areas under the curves of plotted functions helps simplify certain calculations and improve the accuracy of the obtained results. © 2026 The Author(s). AB_raw: This paper explores light interference in physics education and offers a teaching-focused approach to its demonstration experiment and modelling. Light interference is a fundamental wave phenomenon that reveals the nature of light through the redistribution of intensity due to wave superposition. The study highlights the need for simple, accessible methods to improve students’ understanding and address common misconceptions about wave optics. The authors present a demonstration experiment using readily available materials: powdered sugar particles on glass plates of varying thicknesses, and a helium-neon laser (λ = 0.6328 μm). This setup enables the observation of interference rings in both reflected and transmitted light, making the phenomenon demonstrable. The theoretical model, grounded in interference principles, provides a comprehensive framework for elucidating the impact of glass thickness and particle radius on ring size. The experimental data demonstrate a correlation between ring size and glass thickness, which is consistent with the predictions of theoretical calculations. From an pedagogical standpoint, the proposed demonstration experiment is uncomplicated, readily accessible, and integrates qualitative and quantitative analysis. It facilitates the development of analytical skills in students by utilising tools such as ImageJ and Mathcad. The implementation of this demonstration experiment can be adaptable to diverse learning levels. It enhances comprehension of the physical nature of the interference phenomenon, stimulates interest in optics, and can be adapted to other powders, including medical powder, talc, and cocoa. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: The rising pitch heard during water-bottle filling is a simple yet instructive example of resonance in a time-varying fluid–air system. This study presents a theoretical analysis of the relationship between water height, discharge rate, and sound frequency by modelling the bottle as a closed-end organ pipe. As the bottle fills, the water–air interface rises and continuously shortens the air column, which acts as a variable-length resonator whose fundamental frequency increases accordingly. Using an idealised, monotonically decreasing volumetric inflow (taken here as linear in time) and neglecting turbulence and Doppler effects, we derive an analytical frequency–time expression. The resulting function predicts a nonlinear frequency increase consistent with standing-wave physics in a compressible medium. For representative parameters H = 0.23 m, A = 3.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, and c = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>, the predicted pitch evolution aligns with everyday observations of bottle filling. Although the governing equation reduces to a Chini-type form that does not generally admit a closed-form solution, a series approximation provides useful insight into its behaviour. The model clarifies how fluid filling kinematics sets a time-dependent acoustic boundary condition, offering an accessible theoretical context for teaching resonance in physics. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This study investigates how GeoGebra and PhET simulations are integrated into mathematics and physics curricula in rural and urban Rwandan lower secondary schools, focusing on both the opportunities they present and the challenges teachers encounter. AB_raw: In quantum circuits, qubits and the quantum gates acting on them have traditionally been analysed using matrix algebra and Dirac notation. While powerful, these can be unintuitive for conceptual understanding and rapid problem solving. In this work, a new schematic representation method is developed that visualizes the effects of quantum gates on qubits without relying on complex mathematical operations. In the new notation, quantum bits (qubits) are represented using black (|0〉) and white (|1〉) circles. When a quantum gate is applied to a qubit, the circle representing the qubit is visually modified. For example, a Hadamard gate transforms a solid black or white circle into a half-black and half-white circle representing superposition. The work shows how this method simplifies the visualization of quantum algorithms, entanglement, and multi- qubit operations. The work proposes how this method can act as a visual aid to support the understanding of quantum algorithms, entanglement, and multi-qubit operations. Thus, the initial conceptual analysis of basic quantum circuits can be facilitated by simple schematic representations, reducing the immediate cognitive load of complex mathematical operations for beginners. © 2026 The Author(s). TI: ANALOGICAL MODELS TO INTRODUCE HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS TO MODERN PHYSICS: AN INQUIRY-BASED ACTIVITY ON RUTHERFORD’S GOLD FOIL EXPERIMENT
AB_raw: This study presents the design and the implementation of an inquiry-based reconstruction of Rutherford’s gold foil experiment. The activity engaged students in collaborative exploration using a ‘black box’ as an analogical model of the atom. Grounded in constructivist theory and the Focus-Action-Reflection model to introduce analogies in the in-class context, we explore how analogical reasoning can support high school students in understanding the atomic structure. Data from student worksheets, graphical representations, and group discussions were analyzed using thematic, phenomenographic, and conceptual metaphor analysis. Results indicate that students were able to develop and refine analogical models, reason from empirical evidence, and engage in critical reflection on the epistemological limits of the analogy. While students demonstrated conceptual gains and collaborative problem-solving, the analysis also revealed persistent risks of reifying metaphors or overextending macroscopic analogies to quantum domains. These findings highlight the value—and limitations—of structured analogical modeling in contemporary physics education, and point to the need for teacher training that fosters epistemological awareness and reflective use of models in the classroom. © 2025 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd.

AB_raw: This study employed a low-cost method for quantifying bouncing ball dynamics with smartphone video. High-speed video analysis was used to investigate the bouncing behaviour of different balls, including table tennis, rubber, and tennis balls, on a table tennis surface. To examine the effect of surface material on bouncing dynamics, the table tennis ball was also tested on wood and tile surfaces. Key parameters analysed included bounce height decay, the coefficient of restitution (COR), and the bounce half-life. Additionally, we measured the total bouncing time and analysed the relationship between changes in gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, and total mechanical energy (ME). Our results revealed a significant correlation between the COR and the decay rate of bounce height. Balls with higher COR values, indicative of lower energy loss per bounce, exhibited slower decay rates, resulting in longer bounce half-lives and extended total bounce times. For instance, the table tennis ball on a tile surface demonstrated a high COR of 0.93, a bounce half-life of 4.65 bounces, and a total bounce time of 8.22 ± 0.34 s. This suggests that material properties such as stiffness and elasticity of both the ball and the surface significantly influence the COR and decay rate, beyond just surface smoothness. Furthermore, our analysis of ME changes in the bouncing balls aligns with theoretical predictions, providing insights into the energy transformations occurring during bouncing. This improved understanding can also be a valuable tool for educators, helping teachers and students bridge the gap between theory and real-world observations, leading to a deeper grasp of the concepts. © 2024 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: WEIGHTLESSNESS IN A BOTTLE
AB_raw: A simple method of demonstrating apparent weightlessness in free fall is described. The Apollo 15 hammer and feather drop experiment can be recreated in the classroom using a book to shield the feather from air resistance. Plastic toys and a feather thrown together in a plastic bottle can be used to recreate an apparent weightless environment close to the surface of the Earth. Since the bottle follows a parabolic trajectory, the objects within also follow a parabolic path and are seen to float as if in a space ship in orbit around the Earth. This demonstration is useful for demonstrating to students that apparent weightlessness is not confined to outer space. The use of toy fish in the experiments makes a connection with the neutral buoyancy training of astronauts. The experiments also exemplify Newton’s second law that force is mass times acceleration. © 2024 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd.

AB_raw: The photoelectric effect, which reveals the emission of electrons from material when exposed to light, is a foundational experiment in quantum physics that elucidates the interaction between light and matter. However, the lack of laboratory equipment and the difficulty of the experiment frequently prevent its conduct in educational settings. To address these challenges, this study developed and validated a virtual reality (VR) prototype designed to simulate the photoelectric effect experiment. The VR tool enables students to manipulate key variables such as light frequency and intensity, observe electron emission, and investigate the responses of various metals in real-time. The study adopted a research and development methodology, which involved iterative design, development, and validation by a panel of experts. The prototype was assessed on criteria including accuracy, educational value, and usability. The results indicate that the VR prototype accurately simulates the photoelectric effect. Validation data confirmed the educational effectiveness of the tool, which received high ratings for engagement and visual quality. While VR offers a flexible, scalable, and safe environment for exploring complex quantum phenomena, it is positioned as a complementary tool to enhance, rather than replace, traditional laboratory experiences. This approach is particularly valuable for institutions and high schools where expensive equipment may not be available. Future work will focus on expanding the scope of the VR tool to cover additional quantum experiments and improving user comfort to ensure broader accessibility for diverse educational settings. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: The ammeter–voltmeter method is a classic approach for determining electrical resistance, widely used in educational and laboratory contexts. However, it may be presented under idealized assumptions that disregard the internal resistance of measuring instruments. This simplification, frequently found in both textbooks and circuit simulators, can lead to inaccurate measurements and overlook important experimental considerations. To address this gap, this study investigates how the internal resistance of voltmeters and ammeters affects resistance measurement accuracy and how virtual instruments can be adapted to more realistically emulate physical laboratory conditions. Using Tinkercad, we characterized the internal resistance of the simulator’s default virtual multimeters and implemented modifications to simulate quasi-real multimeters with internal resistance. These modified instruments were applied in several configurations of the ammeter–voltmeter method to evaluate their influence on the measurement of resistors of varying magnitudes. Results show that measurement accuracy is highly sensitive to the configuration used and to the relationship between the internal resistances of the instruments and the unknown resistor. Conditions were identified under which each setup provides accurate or distorted results, including cases where either current division or additional voltage drops lead to systematic errors. This work indicates the importance of modeling instrument limitations, even in virtual environments, to better represent the complexity of real-world measurements. The proposed simulation approach may be particularly useful in scenarios with limited laboratory access or as a tool to prepare for or reflect upon physical experiments. © 2025 The Author(s). TI: SYSTEMATIC HEAT LOSS IN OPEN CALORIMETRIC SYSTEMS: A MODELLING-BASED APPROACH TO TEACHING ENTHALPY
AB_raw: Laboratory activities aimed at teaching thermodynamic concepts often rely on simplified experimental setups, particularly in educational contexts with limited resources. One common consequence of such conditions is the appearance of systematic discrepancies between theoretical and experimental values, especially when calorimetric measurements are performed using open or imperfect systems. This paper analyses a set of temperature measurements obtained from the dissolution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in water using improvised calorimeters. Rather than seeking to optimise calorimetric accuracy, the study characterises the systematic error inherent to open systems and examines its potential pedagogical significance in the teaching of enthalpy. A simple model incorporating a corrective term, (Formula presented) (Formula presented), is introduced to represent heat losses to the environment. The analysis suggests that non-ideal experimental conditions can provide a structured context for discussing systematic error, model assumptions and non-ideal behaviour in thermodynamics. In addition, an open-access web application is presented to facilitate exploratory analysis of how variations in temperature measurements influence calculated enthalpy values. The work constitutes a theoretically grounded instructional proposal based on experimental analysis and illustrates how a modelling framework can support reflective discussion of systematic error in resource-limited laboratory settings. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: TRADITIONAL ARCHITECTURE INTEGRATION IN PHYSICS: CENTER OF MASS, IMPULSE, AND TORQUE IN TRADITIONAL LIMAS HOUSE ARCHITECTURE
AB_raw: The principles of physics can be applied to traditional architecture as part of efforts to preserve local wisdom. This study investigates several physics principles of the Limas house, a traditional structure from Palembang, South Sumatera, Indonesia. A descriptive qualitative method was used, with data collected through observations, interviews, and documentation from the Balaputradewa Museum in South Sumatra. The interviews revealed that several physics concepts, including center of mass and material density, are intuitively applied in the construction of the Limas house. The study calculated the volume of the house to be 5040 m<sup>3</sup>, and the center of mass of the house was determined to be at the coordinate point (x = 9.81 m, y = 9.19 m, z = 3.87 m), relative to the surface of the main room. A lower center of mass will enhance the stability of the building by evenly distributing the load to the foundation, while the impulse depends on the surface area affected by the force. Torque requires strong connections to withstand rotational forces and prevent damage. These findings suggest that the principles of physics can aid in the analysis of the construction. This third element supports the design in architecture and the stability of the Limas house. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. TI: EXPLORING THE POTENTIAL OF CHATGPT FOR FEEDBACK AND EVALUATION IN EXPERIMENTAL PHYSICS
AF: ABREU MARCOS;SUÁREZ ALVARO;STARI CECILIA;MARTI ARTURO C
AB_raw: Recent advances in large language models have opened new possibilities for Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted grading in higher education. This study explores the use of a GPT-5.4–based system to support the evaluation of introductory physics laboratory reports using a rubric-driven automated workflow implemented in batch mode via API. AI-generated scores were compared with instructor grading, and the feedback was analysed qualitatively across rubric criteria. The results show weak agreement in the ranking of reports and noticeable differences at the level of individual scores. Item-level analysis indicates that the model frequently produced feedback classified as correct application but also generated a non-negligible proportion of reasonable but superficial responses and invalid evaluations. These limitations were mainly associated with restricted access to evidence during text extraction and OCR, particularly for equations, figures, and graphical representations. The findings suggest that batch-based AI grading can provide systematic feedback and help identify recurring patterns in student work, supporting instructors in large-scale courses. However, under the conditions examined, AI-generated scores were not interchangeable with instructor grading and should be understood as a tool to assist, rather than replace, the evaluation process. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: For several years, the educational gap in certain Latin American countries and around the world has become increasingly evident. The limited access to cutting-edge knowledge and technologies to strengthen student training processes has emerged as a significant problem, leading to increased inequality in job opportunities in these regions and progressive setbacks in social and economic development. One way to mitigate this problem has been to provide access to information through telecommunications. However, integration with educational processes has been deficient, especially in the areas of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. This work proposes the development of a remote physics laboratory platform for experimental validation of models explaining certain physical phenomena. This platform is based on the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm, allowing students and teachers to connect with these experiences coveringtopics in mechanics, electricity and magnetism, optics, and thermodynamics from remote regions. These laboratories utilize physical setups in educational institutions that have been modified to provide connectivity and remote control capabilities based on IoT. Finally, a framework for implementing new remote laboratories based on the IoT paradigm through an open-source platform is presented. The system has been tested and validated with high school and early university students to verify its usefulness, showing the potential to enhance educational processes by providing laboratory access to students and teachers from primary education to secondary education and university-level professional programs. © 2024 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This paper presents a study of Faraday’s law of induction, using an experimental apparatus based on the ESP32 microcontroller, adopting a practical and pedagogical approach. The setup enables real-time acquisition and both qualitative and quantitative analysis of the behaviours of current, magnetic field, and induced voltage. This enables clear visualization of how the induced voltage is related to the temporal variation of the magnetic field, as described by Faraday’s law. The methodology facilitates the understanding of concepts that are often regarded as abstract and difficult for students to grasp, making them more accessible and intuitive. The integration of the experiment with Excel, employing PLX-DAQ software, provides a customized tool for this application, enabling streamlined data acquisition and analysis. The promising results obtained in this study highlight the potential of using microcontrollers as a valuable pedagogical resource in physics education, capable of fostering more active learning by linking theoretical principles with practical applications. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: Understanding the concept of hydrogen emission spectrum in intermediate physics is challenging because students must connect observed spectral lines to abstract atomic models. This study investigates whether virtual reality (VR) laboratories improve conceptual understanding more than conventional teaching does and which cognitive processes, as revised by Bloom’s taxonomy, are most improved. The quasi-experimental, quantitative, pretest–posttest, control-group design involved 216 twelfth-grade students from three schools (108 in the virtual-reality group and 108 in the control group). A 30-item, validated test measured interpretation, example giving, classification, summarization, explanation, inference, and comparison. Learning improvement was quantified using normalized improvement (N-gain). The VR group had high normalized gains across all indicators, with the largest gains in summarizing (g = 0.882) and interpreting (g = 0.875), followed by strong gains in inferring (g = 0.829) and classifying (g = 0.806). The control group had high increases in interpreting (g = 0.906) and summarizing (g = 0.882), and moderate increases in giving examples (g = 0.602), inferring (g = 0.620), and comparing (g = 0.569). Since the score distribution was not normal (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p < 0.001), within-group improvement was tested using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while between-group differences were tested using the Mann–Whitney U test. Both groups improved significantly (Wilcoxon Z = − 9.026, p < 0.001 for each group) and baseline equivalence was confirmed (U = 58 161.5, Z = − 0.034, p = 0.973). Posttest performance was better in the VR group (mean rank: 133.57 vs 83.43; U: 3,124.00; Z: −5.970; p: <0.001). These results suggest that VR laboratories can improve conceptual understanding and strengthen cognitive processes oriented toward reasoning when learning about the hydrogen emission spectrum. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. For quantitative contrast evaluation, effective analysis can be achieved by applying 15 kV and 30 kV for 4 s, while minimizing radiation. At 30 kV, prolonged exposure times should be avoided because of increased radiation. This experimental setup provides an effective introduction to x-ray usage for beginners. This study provides guidelines for optimizing the applied voltage and exposure time in the Crookes tube to enhance the experimental outcomes while ensuring safety. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: Quantum physics plays a central role in contemporary science and technology, while school textbooks mediate curriculum intentions and classroom practice. This study examines how quantum physics concepts are represented in Greek upper secondary physics and chemistry textbooks. A qualitative content analysis was conducted on the officially prescribed student textbooks used in all three grades of the Greek General Lyceum. The analysis investigated the presence, distribution, pedagogical framing, and cross-disciplinary coherence of quantum concepts across subjects and grade levels. The findings indicate that quantum content is largely absent in the first two grades of physics and becomes concentrated in the final grade, where it is predominantly presented descriptively. In chemistry, quantum concepts appear earlier but are mainly embedded within application-oriented discussions of atomic structure. Across both subjects, probabilistic and epistemological dimensions receive limited attention, and cross-disciplinary alignment remains weak. These patterns suggest that quantum theory is presented through parallel disciplinary trajectories rather than as an integrated conceptual framework. © 2026 The Author(s). AB_raw: In this work, we present a didactic experiment involving the observation of forced oscillations in the vertical plane induced by an electric force acting on a dielectric cylinder that forms part of a mass-spring system. The cylinder is placed on a homemade Leyden jar-type capacitor, which is charged over time by a Van de Graaff-type electrostatic generator. Simultaneously, the motion of the cylinder is recorded using a smartphone camera, and the video is later analysed with the Tracker software. During the recording, the generator is switched on for a period, then turned off, and finally, the capacitor is discharged. We developed a simplified theoretical model to describe the cylinder's motion during the three regimes, allowing us to understand the forced oscillations and the displacement of the system's stable equilibrium position immediately after the generator is switched on. In the regime of small oscillations, we demonstrate that the system behaves as a forced oscillator with variable frequency when the charge generator is active, due to the coupling between the system's time-dependent charges and the cylinder's displacement. Finally, we use the modelling, combined with video analysis, to show the possibility of obtaining an estimate of the product of the charges that remain in the system immediately after the generator is turned off, even when detecting displacements on the order of the experimental uncertainty limit of 1 mm. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: This study aims to evaluate the generalizability of the rolling motion model proposed by Wibowo et al (2025) by extending its application to a different class of rolling objects, namely plastic cups. The investigation focuses on comparing theoretical and experimental turning radii of circular trajectories formed by cups with distinct sizes and geometries. Four plastic cups—green, blue-patterned, yellow, and dark green—differing in size, shape, and mass were tested. Theoretical radii were calculated based on geometric parameters, while experimental radii were obtained by tracing the cups’ rolling paths. The theoretical values (R<sub>t</sub>) were 35.90 cm (green), 38.88 cm (blue-patterned), 23.69 cm (yellow), and 68.01 cm (dark green), compared with experimental results (R<sub>e</sub>) of 39.09 cm, 40.14 cm, 25.64 cm, and 63.04 cm, respectively. The relative errors ranged from 3.23% to 8.89%, indicating strong consistency and confirming the robustness of the geometric model. Nevertheless, the results also revealed systematic deviations, with larger cups producing tighter curves than predicted, largely due to asymmetric mass distribution and rotational inertia that are not accounted for in the geometric formulation. These findings highlight the limitations of a purely geometric approach while demonstrating that the model remains a reliable approximation for a broader class of rolling objects. In addition to its theoretical contribution, the study underscores the pedagogical value of the rolling cup experiment, offering students a low-cost and engaging activity to explore rotational dynamics, geometric modelling, and error analysis while reflecting on the interplay between idealized models and real-world observations. © 2025 IOP Publishing Ltd. AB_raw: Understanding how learners define and mentally model thermodynamic concepts is essential for meaningful conceptual development. This study examined pre-service science teachers’ definitional knowledge of heat, temperature, and internal energy; their model-based explanations across multiple thermal contexts; and the coherence between these two forms of knowledge. Data were collected from written responses to a five-item open-ended assessment administered to forty-eight participants. Qualitative content analysis was conducted using a coding framework informed by conceptual change perspectives, model-based reasoning, and representational approaches. The analysis of definitions revealed three levels of understanding: conceptual confusion, partially correct but relationally inconsistent explanations, and scientifically accurate yet not fully integrated descriptions. Most participants demonstrated transitional patterns, using correct terminology without establishing mechanistic relationships. Explanations generated for contextual thermal problems produced three types of mental models: fragmented single-variable models, context-dependent hybrid models, and integrated macro–micro–symbolic models. Only one participant demonstrated a fully integrated model. Cross-analysis indicated a partial alignment between definitional levels and mental model types. Crucially, correct definitions did not reliably predict coherent causal reasoning across contexts. These findings suggest that learners activate different cognitive resources depending on the thermal situation, even when they can reproduce scientific terminology. For physics teacher education, this implies a shift from definition-focused instruction to model construction, model comparison, and explicit coordination of macro–micro–symbolic representations. © 2026 The Author(s). AB_raw: In physics education, the electricity and magnetism high school curriculum in Austria includes learning abstract concepts, such as static electric and magnetic fields, and their interactions with matter. This is different to learning about electric circuits at middle-school level, which has been researched extensively. The difficulties in learning such abstract concepts have been studied mostly at undergraduate introductory and advanced levels, with a few exceptions in high school. The objective of this study is to diagnose Austrian high school students' understanding of electric and magnetic fields and interactions and identify their most common difficulties. To achieve this objective, we conducted a study with a mixed methods approach with a concurrent triangulation design. The participants were 265 high school students in Austria, who answered a multiple-choice questionnaire and open-ended questions on several topics of electricity and magnetism. We found that students have difficulties with using and interpreting the field representations, such as creating hybrid representations of field lines and vector arrows. Both in the quantitative and qualitative results, the confusion between electricity and magnetism was evident: in electricity, students would treat the electric field as magnetic field, and in magnetism, the students would treat magnets as charged poles. © 2025 Institute of Physics.
